content: Vegan Outreach is an American organization dedicated to advocating for animal rights by exposing and working to end animal cruelty. They achieve this through the widespread distribution of informational booklets. By October 2006, over five million hard copies of their brochures had been distributed globally by local members of the organization. The founders of Vegan Outreach, Matt Ball and Jack Norris, first met in Cincinnati, Ohio, in 1990. As members of the Animal Rights Community of Cincinnati, they, along with Phil Murray (now co-owner of Pangea Vegan Products), organized fur protests during the winter of 1990-1991 outside cultural events. By 1992, their focus shifted to vegetarianism, and the group funded the printing and distribution of 10,000 pro-vegetarian flyers titled Vegetarianism. In June 1993, twelve activists, including Matt and Jack, held a three-day Fast for Farm Animals in front of a Cincinnati slaughterhouse. This fast symbolized the three days of starvation many animals endure before slaughter. On the final day, some protesters displayed a large banner reading Stop Eating Animals at the University of Cincinnati campus. While the fast garnered some media attention, the activists felt the banner display was the most impactful part of the event. Following this, Matt and Jack formed Animal Liberation Action (ALA) and began a campaign of holding Stop Eating Animals banners on street corners. This approach laid the groundwork for Vegan Outreach's current strategy of disseminating information on college campuses and in other high-traffic areas. In 1994, ALA developed a booklet titled And Justice For All, which highlighted the reasons for adopting a vegan diet, including the abuse of animals, the environmental impact of industrial farming, and the health benefits of plant-based eating. In 1995, ALA officially changed its name to Vegan Outreach and shifted its focus from banner campaigns, which were often poorly received, to distributing printed booklets. That same year, a revised booklet titled Vegan Outreach was printed, with the initial 10,000 copies assembled by hand to save costs. In the fall of 1995, Jack Norris toured the Midwestern United States, distributing the booklet at 19 universities. In 1996, Vegan Outreach published the first Why Vegan? booklet, which was distributed at 171 colleges that year. Jack continued traveling to distribute materials until funds ran out in 1997. He then decided to become a Registered Dietitian, dedicating three years to education and an internship to better understand nutrition science and address the challenges faced by failed vegetarians. In June 1998, Vegan Outreach published a lengthy article titled Veganism as the Path to Animal Liberation (later renamed Activism and Veganism Reconsidered). This essay critiqued the animal rights movement's focus on protests and civil disobedience, arguing that exposing factory farms and promoting veganism were more effective strategies. It emphasized that widespread adoption of veganism was essential for meaningful progress in animal liberation. The essay had a significant impact on activists and shaped Vegan Outreach's advocacy principles. In 1999 and 2000, new booklets were developed, including the Vegetarian Starter Guide (now Guide to Cruelty-Free Eating) and Vegetarian Living (now Try Vegetarian). These materials were designed for individuals interested in vegetarianism and avoided the graphic imagery found in the Why Vegan? brochure. By 2001, over 330,000 copies of Why Vegan? and Vegetarian Living were distributed. Vegan Outreach's Adopt-A-College program began in 2003, focusing on distributing booklets at colleges across the U.S. and Canada. In its first year, 22,000 brochures were distributed at 63 schools. By the fall of 2006, 344,000 brochures had been distributed at 385 schools. Vegan Outreach hired Jon Camp as a full-time employee in 2004, and he distributed over 145,000 brochures in his first two years. In 2005, the organization introduced a new brochure titled Even If You Like Meat, which aimed to address the misconception that reducing animal cruelty required an all-or-nothing approach. The brochure emphasized that any reduction in animal product consumption helps prevent suffering. To overcome the challenge of people dismissing their flyers as mere health advice, Vegan Outreach included images of factory farms on the cover of Even If You Like Meat to highlight the serious social issue of animal cruelty. Contrary to initial concerns, this approach increased the acceptance rate of the brochures. By 2006, Vegan Outreach had hired two additional full-time leafleters, Victor Tsou and Jenna Calabrese, to cover the western and northeastern United States, respectively. Anne Green was hired as the organization's vice president in 2007 after years of unofficial contributions to its planning and management. Today, Vegan Outreach continues its mission of distributing information on college campuses and other busy venues worldwide. Their brochures have been distributed in all 50 U.S. states, Puerto Rico, ten Canadian provinces and territories, Mexico, and numerous other countries, including Australia, Austria, Brazil, Denmark, Egypt, England, Finland, France, Germany, India, Ireland, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Singapore, Slovenia, Slovakia, Spain, Sri Lanka, South Africa, and Taiwan. Many of their materials are available in multiple languages, thanks to volunteer translation efforts. Vegan Outreach's mission is to reduce suffering in the world by focusing on people's food choices. They emphasize this for three main reasons: the vast number of animals raised and killed for food annually, the intense suffering experienced by farmed animals, and the accessibility of promoting ethical eating as a means to reduce animal suffering. Their materials advocate for reducing and eventually eliminating animal products from one's diet, offering alternative food suggestions, nutritional information, and advocacy tips. Vegan Outreach encourages individuals to focus on reducing animal cruelty rather than obsessing over personal dietary minutiae. They believe that inspiring others to change their habits has a far greater impact than individual veganism alone. The organization prioritizes outreach to college students for three reasons: their relative openness to change, the long-term impact of their choices, and the ability to reach large numbers of students efficiently. Vegan Outreach's grassroots approach ensures that each person who interacts with their materials receives comprehensive information to consider in their own time. By inspiring even one person to change, hundreds of animals can be spared from suffering on factory farms. Vegan Outreach emphasizes the importance of being effective advocates rather than simply righteous vegans, striving to inspire others through compassion, respect, and joy.
